query: The Shelf of Old Theses {Along the back wall run three centuries of finished theses, bound in cloth that has faded to the same brown.|The thesis shelf. You've started a list of the best titles. Today's find: a study of the emotional lives of doorknobs.|The old theses. You can find the good ones by feel now: the spines are worn where people keep taking them down.} {One near the end has a pressed flower for a bookmark.|One has a note on the flyleaf: "Passed. Barely. Worth it."|{season == "spring": Blossom drifts in through the open window and settles on the spines.|A spider has made its home between two famous ones.}} Read a famous one {It's brilliant, and it was written by someone younger than you. You put it back very carefully and go and sit somewhere quiet.|It's the one everybody cites. Reading it in full is like seeing a mountain from the bottom.|You read the most-worn one cover to cover. It's so good it hurts, which you suppose is the point.} Read a gloriously bad one {It argues for forty pages that rain is a kind of apology. It passed. You feel enormously better about everything.|You read the doorknob one. It is three hundred pages long and completely serious, and you laugh until the carrels shush you.|You find one with footnotes longer than its chapters, and footnotes to the footnotes. Your own thesis suddenly seems sane.}
